label: Chapter 6: Leopold's Capital, the Belle Époque and the Congo, 1831 to 1914

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The new Belgium turned out to be a remarkable success story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And Brussels was its showcase.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Belgium was the first country on the European continent to undergo an industrial revolution, following the example of Britain.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Coal and iron in the south, textiles in Flanders, and a good banking system created real wealth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the railways.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1835, the first railway on the continent opened between Brussels and the nearby city of Mechelen, and within a few years, the country had a dense network of tracks, with Brussels at the center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The population grew fast, and the capital swelled with civil servants, bankers, merchants, and workers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It also became a refuge for ideas.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1834, liberal Brussels founded a new university, the Free University of Brussels, dedicated to free inquiry, independent of both state and church.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And because the new Belgian constitution was so liberal, the city attracted writers, thinkers, and political refugees from across Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Baudelaire, Victor Hugo.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Charles Baudelaire stayed there, and Victor Hugo lived for a time on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1873, in a Brussels hotel room, the poet Paul Verlaine shot and wounded his young lover, the poet Arthur Rimbaud, and then went to jail in Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's dramatic. But one exile, above all, left a mark.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1845, the young German philosopher Karl Marx, expelled from France, came to Brussels with his wife and family, and he stayed until 1848.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With his friend Friedrich Engels, he wrote a pamphlet in Brussels, in the winter of 1847 and 1848, called the Manifesto of the Communist Party.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Published elsewhere, though.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In London, in February of 1848, and Marx was expelled from Belgium a few weeks later.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The pamphlet he wrote there went on to shape the history of the twentieth century.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile, the river had become a problem.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A disaster. The Senne, which had made Brussels possible, ran through the middle of the city, an open sewer, choked with refuse, and it flooded regularly.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It carried cholera. The stench in summer was notorious.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So they buried it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the eighteen-sixties, the city's reforming mayor, Jules Anspach, decided to bury it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between 1867 and 1871, the river was covered with a long brick vault, and above it, the city built a grand new avenue lined with elegant buildings, modeled on the Paris boulevards of Baron Haussmann.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Boulevard Anspach.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After the mayor who built it. The river is still there today, flowing in a tunnel beneath the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They built a Stock Exchange, the Bourse, in the heart of the new district, and the whole center was transformed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It sounds like a triumph.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was an enormous achievement, and also a loss.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Hundreds of old houses and streets in the working-class neighborhoods were torn down, and whole communities were uprooted.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there was another giant project, the Palace of Justice.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1866, work began on a vast new Palace of Justice, designed by the architect Joseph Poelaert, on a hill above the Marolles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: When it was finished in 1883, it was often described as the largest building constructed anywhere in the nineteenth century, a colossal mass of columns, domes, and staircases that dwarfs the city around it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the neighbors weren't thrilled.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To build it, authorities flattened part of the old working-class Marolles district.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Locals have grumbled about it ever since.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Now, we get to Leopold the Second.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1865, Leopold the First died, and his son took the throne as Leopold the Second.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He reigned for forty-four years, and he was ambitious in a way his father was not.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He felt that his country was too small, and he dreamed of an empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The great European powers were carving up Africa, and Leopold wanted a piece of it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And this is a hard part of the story.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It is. At a conference in Berlin in 1884 and 1885, the great powers recognized Leopold as the ruler of a vast territory in central Africa, about eighty times the size of Belgium.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This territory was not a Belgian colony.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was the king's personal property, called the Congo Free State.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And what followed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the worst atrocities of the colonial era.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Leopold's agents forced villagers to collect rubber and ivory, under a system of terror: hostages were taken, villages burned, and people who failed to meet quotas were beaten, mutilated, or killed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians estimate that millions of Congolese died from violence, starvation, and disease during these years, although the exact numbers are debated.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: How did the world find out?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Reports by missionaries, journalists, and the British diplomat Roger Casement, and a campaign led by the journalist Edmund Morel, eventually produced an international outcry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1908, under heavy pressure, the Belgian state took over the colony from the king, and it became the Belgian Congo, which Belgium ruled until 1960.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that money ended up in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Partly. The money that Leopold drew from the Congo went partly into building, and into impressing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He built the great Cinquantenaire park and its triumphal arch, to commemorate fifty years of Belgian independence.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He built wide avenues, such as Avenue Louise, and monuments, and royal greenhouses at Laeken, and a huge museum of Central Africa in the suburb of Tervuren.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the world's fair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the Brussels world's fair of 1897, he organized a colonial exhibition in which Congolese people were put on display in a replica village.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The grand showpiece of Belgium's capital had been paid for, in part, by a terrible human cost, and that's a story Brussels has been grappling with ever since.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile, something very different was happening in architecture.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the eighteen-nineties, a group of young architects, led by Victor Horta, created a new style that rejected the heavy historical imitations of the time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They used iron, glass, and sweeping curves inspired by plants and flowers, in what came to be known as Art Nouveau, or the new art.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Tassel house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1893 and 1894, Horta built a townhouse for a professor named Emile Tassel, in which iron columns shaped like stems and stairs twining like vines flowed through the whole house, with light pouring in from above.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's widely regarded as the first Art Nouveau building.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Others followed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Paul Hankar and Henry van de Velde, among others.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The style spread to Paris, Vienna, and Barcelona, but it started in Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Several of Horta's townhouses are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So by 1900, what kind of city is Brussels?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A prosperous, confident metropolis of more than half a million people in its wider urban area, a city of cafés, department stores, glass-roofed shopping arcades, and boulevards.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was also a French-speaking city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the time of independence, a large share of ordinary Brusselers spoke a Dutch dialect, but French was the language of government, business, education, and prestige, and over the nineteenth century, it steadily took over.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And today it's officially bilingual.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the question of language, which was just beginning to stir in the late nineteenth century, will return again and again in the story of modern Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the fates of small countries rest on the decisions of large ones.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The guarantee of Belgian neutrality, signed in 1839, was now seventy-five years old.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in the summer of 1914, a crisis in the Balkans pushed Europe toward war.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Germany's plan to defeat France called for an army to march through neutral Belgium.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: If someone wants to see this chapter in stone?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk the Boulevard Anspach and look at the grand facades of the Bourse.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Visit the Palace of Justice, whose terrace has a famous view over the whole city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And if you have time for one museum, make it the Horta Museum in Saint-Gilles, the house where the architect lived and worked.
